title: Activation Functions: ReLU & Friends
hook: Stack linear layers and you still just have one linear layer. The nonlinearity between them is what gives a network its power.
key_points: Without a nonlinearity, stacked layers collapse into a single linear transformation.
ReLU, max(0, x), is the cheap, fast default that made deep networks practical.
Sigmoid and tanh squash outputs into a range but can saturate and stall gradients.
GELU and other variants trade a little cost for smoother behavior, common in transformers.
content_html: An activation function is the nonlinear step applied to each neuron's output, and it's the ingredient that lets neural networks model complex relationships. Without it, no matter how many layers you stack, the whole thing reduces to a single linear function. ReLU is the popular default, with sigmoid, tanh, and GELU as common alternatives.
extra_html:
How it works

Each layer computes a weighted sum, then passes it through an activation. ReLU simply zeroes out negatives and keeps positives — cheap to compute and resistant to the vanishing-gradient problem that plagues sigmoid and tanh, whose flat tails can choke the gradients that training relies on. Smoother functions like GELU are widely used in transformer models where their shape helps.

Why it matters

The choice of activation affects how easily and how deeply a network trains. ReLU's simplicity was a big reason very deep networks became trainable at all. Knowing why nonlinearity is non-negotiable — and what each option's tradeoffs are — is foundational to understanding why architectures look the way they do.

flashcards.prompt: What makes ReLU resistant to the problem that plagues sigmoid and tanh?

choices.text: It doesn't saturate, so it avoids the vanishing-gradient problem
It squashes outputs into a bounded range
It is more expensive but smoother to compute

flashcards.explanation_html: Sigmoid and tanh have flat tails that choke gradients; ReLU simply zeroes negatives and keeps positives, resisting vanishing gradients.

flashcards.prompt: Which activation is commonly used in transformer models for its smoother shape?
flashcards.explanation_html: Smoother functions like GELU trade a little cost for smoother behavior and are widely used in transformers.
